script.opening: "Hi — so I keep getting these horrible headaches, but the weird thing is they start with my vision going funny, like flickering zigzag lines down one side, for about twenty minutes, and THEN the headache hits. It’s happened three times now. I’m getting married in seven weeks and I can’t be doing with this on my honeymoon, so I really just need something stronger to knock them on the head. Can you sort me out a prescription?"

facts.text: If explored: clear visual aura — zigzag/flickering lines, one side of vision, ~20–30 min, fully reversible, FOLLOWED by a typical one-sided throbbing headache with nausea and light sensitivity. This is migraine WITH aura — new for her (her teenage migraines had no aura).

On the combined pill (oestrogen-containing) for 6 years. Crucially — migraine WITH aura + combined pill substantially raises ischaemic stroke risk; this is a hard contraindication (UKMEC 4). She has NOT connected the aura to the pill and assumes the pill is irrelevant.

HIDDEN AGENDA — reachable when the plan to stop the pill emerges: she relies on the pill to control heavy, painful periods AND, far more pressingly, she is getting married in 7 weeks and is terrified of an unplanned pregnancy / bleeding or pain ruining the wedding and honeymoon. "Just stop the pill" lands as a catastrophe to her, so she may resist or downplay the aura.
If asked openly and non-judgementally: she’s started smoking again with wedding stress (~5/day), hasn’t mentioned it because she’s embarrassed — another stroke risk multiplier with the combined pill.

Officially: stronger painkillers. Actually (and needs): recognition that the aura makes her current pill genuinely dangerous, a SAFE alternative contraception sorted before the wedding so she’s not exposed, period-pain control, and migraine treatment — without her honeymoon plans collapsing.

ice.ideas: She just has worse headaches now and needs stronger painkillers; the visual stuff is part of the headache and nothing to do with her pill.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — getting married in 7 weeks: terror that stopping the pill means unplanned pregnancy and that heavy/painful periods will wreck the wedding/honeymoon; embarrassment about smoking again.
ice.expectations: A stronger painkiller prescription. What she actually needs: to understand the aura–pill stroke risk, a safe alternative contraceptive sorted promptly, period and migraine management, and smoking support.

cues: "Vision goes funny THEN the headache hits" — textbook migraine WITH aura; the contraception flag is the whole consultation.
"I’m getting married in seven weeks" — the real anxiety; stopping the pill feels like a wedding catastrophe.
Hesitation if asked about smoking — embarrassment, not absence; ask so disclosure is safe.

checkpoints.text: Recognises this as migraine WITH aura (NICE CG150: fully reversible, usually visual aura developing over at least 5 minutes and lasting 5 to 60 minutes, followed by a migraine headache) — NEW for her — and does not treat it as just "worse headaches" needing stronger analgesia

Identifies the critical safety issue: migraine with aura + combined (oestrogen) pill is a hard contraindication (UKMEC 2025: UKMEC 4, an unacceptable health risk, at any age) due to substantially increased ischaemic stroke risk — the combined pill must be STOPPED

Does NOT just stop the pill and leave her exposed: arranges a safe alternative contraceptive promptly (progestogen-only pill, implant, injection, or IUS — all usable with migraine + aura under UKMEC 2025; a progestogen-only pill can usually be started the same day, with condoms until it is effective, timing per CoSRH (formerly FSRH) guidance), explicitly protecting her before the wedding

Addresses the period-control need the pill was meeting (heavy/painful periods): e.g. the levonorgestrel IUS (NICE NG88: the first treatment to consider for heavy menstrual bleeding without identified pathology; warn that bleeding is often irregular at first and benefit can take up to 6 cycles), POP, tranexamic/mefenamic acid for menorrhagia — so she is not left with the problem that put her on the pill

Manages the migraine itself appropriately (NICE CG150): acute treatment (oral triptan with an NSAID or paracetamol, antiemetic), lifestyle/trigger review, headache diary, medication-overuse warning, and consideration of prophylaxis if frequent — avoiding topiramate as a first choice in a woman who may soon want a pregnancy (MHRA Drug Safety Update, June 2024: contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless a Pregnancy Prevention Programme is in place; it also reduces hormonal contraceptive effect) — and screens stroke/secondary red flags (this aura is typical and reversible; flag atypical/persistent neurology)
Asks about smoking non-judgementally and addresses it as a compounding stroke risk with oestrogen; offers cessation support (NICE NG209: referral to stop-smoking services)
Hears the wedding anxiety beneath "something stronger" and frames the contraception switch around protecting her wedding/honeymoon, not disrupting it — so she accepts stopping the pill

Safety-nets clearly: stop the combined pill now and use condoms until the new method is reliable; stroke warning signs (FAST, sudden focal/persistent neurology, thunderclap headache) → 999; arranges prompt contraception review and migraine follow-up before the wedding

worked.txt: "That flickering zigzag in your vision before the headache — that’s called an aura, and it tells me these are migraines with aura. They’re not dangerous in themselves, and we can absolutely treat them. But the aura changes one really important thing, and it’s not the painkillers."

"Here’s the thing I have to be straight with you about: migraine WITH aura and the combined pill together raise the risk of stroke enough that we don’t use them in combination. So the most important thing today isn’t a stronger painkiller — it’s coming off this particular pill. I know that’s not what you rang for, so let’s sort it properly."

"And I can hear the wedding in your voice — you are NOT going to be left unprotected or facing your old periods on your honeymoon, I promise. We just swap to a method without the oestrogen: a progestogen-only pill you could start today, or an implant or coil that also tends to make periods lighter. We’ll have you covered well before the day."

"You went on the pill for heavy, painful periods, so I’m not going to ignore that. The hormonal coil in particular is brilliant for that — lighter, less painful periods AND contraception, no oestrogen. If you’d rather not, we can use the mini-pill plus tablets for the period pain and bleeding. You won’t be back to square one."

"For the migraines themselves: a triptan taken when the headache starts, with an anti-sickness tablet, plus an anti-inflammatory — and a headache diary so we spot triggers (wedding stress is a big one right now). Don’t take painkillers on lots of days a month, because that can cause headaches of its own. If they keep coming we can add a daily preventer — and I’d choose one that’s safe if you’re thinking about a baby after the wedding."

"One gentle question — any chance you’ve picked the cigarettes back up with all the stress? … No judgement — but with the migraines, stopping smoking really cuts the stroke risk, and I’ll help. Practical bits: stop the combined pill now, use condoms until the new method is working, and if you ever get sudden face droop, arm weakness, slurred speech or the worst headache of your life — that’s 999. I’ll book you in this week to set up the new contraception properly."

f.learning: Migraine WITH aura is the single most important contraception-safety flag in general practice: combined with an oestrogen-containing pill it substantially raises ischaemic stroke risk and is a UKMEC 4 (absolute) contraindication — the combined pill must stop. The classic exam trap is to hear "worse headaches, wants stronger painkillers" and miss that the visual aura changes everything. But stopping the pill is only half the task: the examinable skill is NOT leaving her exposed — arrange a safe alternative (POP, implant, injection, IUS) promptly, and address the period problem the pill was treating (the IUS is ideal). Here the hidden agenda is a wedding in 7 weeks and terror of unplanned pregnancy / ruined honeymoon, so frame the switch as protecting the wedding. Treat the migraine (NICE CG150: triptan with an NSAID or paracetamol + antiemetic, diary, prophylaxis if frequent — not topiramate as a first choice for a woman who may want a pregnancy, MHRA June 2024), ask about smoking (a compounding oestrogen-stroke risk) non-judgementally and offer stop-smoking support (NICE NG209), and safety-net for stroke. Migraine WITHOUT aura (her teenage pattern) does not carry the same absolute restriction; check its current category in the UKMEC 2025 table rather than quoting one from memory.

knowledge.guideline: UKMEC 2025 (CoSRH) · NICE CG150 (updated June 2025) · NICE NG88 · NICE NG209 · MHRA Drug Safety Update (June 2024)
knowledge.summary: New migraine with aura in a woman on the combined pill is an absolute contraindication to oestrogen. Stop the combined pill today, and at the same time give her safe contraception, a plan for her periods and migraine treatment.

points.t: NICE CG150: aura is reversible, usually visual (zigzag lines, flickering, a blind spot), develops over at least 5 minutes and lasts 5 to 60 minutes, then a migraine headache follows. Hers fits exactly. It is new: her teenage migraines had no aura.
UKMEC 2025: migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 (unacceptable health risk) for combined hormonal contraception at any age, because of the increased risk of ischaemic stroke. The combined pill must stop.

Progestogen-only methods (pill, implant, injection) and the LNG-IUS can be used with migraine with aura. A progestogen-only pill can usually be started straight away; use condoms until the new method is effective, timing per CoSRH guidance.

points.h: Remember why she was on the pill
points.t: NICE NG88: the LNG-IUS is the first treatment to consider for heavy menstrual bleeding without identified pathology. Warn that bleeding is often irregular in the first few cycles and that benefits may take up to 6 cycles. If she declines, NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid or tranexamic acid can be used.

NICE CG150: offer an oral triptan with an NSAID or paracetamol, and consider an antiemetic. Take the triptan when the headache starts. Keep a headache diary and warn about medication-overuse headache. For prevention, CG150 lists propranolol, topiramate or amitriptyline.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (June 2024): topiramate is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women of childbearing potential unless a Pregnancy Prevention Programme is in place. It also reduces the effect of hormonal contraception. For a woman about to marry, it is a poor first choice.
Smoking adds to stroke risk. Ask without judgement and offer stop-smoking support (NICE NG209).

dg.d: Open question; let her describe the aura in her own words; acknowledged the wedding without accepting “just stronger painkillers”.
Wedding in seven weeks, stress, relapse into smoking, reliance on the pill for heavy periods.
Blood pressure check at the contraception review; no imaging needed for typical aura; headache diary.
Migraine with aura vs TIA vs secondary headache; checked for atypical, prolonged or motor aura and thunderclap onset.
Screened for persistent or motor aura, speech disturbance and sudden severe headache; identified the oestrogen stroke risk.
Named migraine with aura and UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Stop the combined pill today; progestogen-only pill now with condoms; LNG-IUS option after the wedding; triptan plus NSAID or paracetamol plus antiemetic.
Heavy periods (tranexamic or mefenamic acid; LNG-IUS per NICE NG88); smoking cessation; topiramate avoided.
Stroke symptoms mean 999; nurse appointment this week; review before the wedding; headache diary; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “vision goes funny, then the headache”, “seven weeks” and the hesitation about smoking.
Idea (stress headaches, pill irrelevant), concern (pregnancy or heavy periods ruining the wedding), expectation (stronger analgesia).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — getting married in 7 weeks: terror that stopping the pill means unplanned pregnancy and that heavy/painful periods will wreck the wedding/honeymoon; embarrassment about smoking again — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Robyn, it’s Dr Lee. I understand you’ve been having headaches. Tell me about them from the beginning.
model.why: Open question; lets her describe the aura herself

model.text: They start with my vision going funny — flickering zigzag lines down one side, for about twenty minutes — and then the headache hits. Three times now. I’m getting married in seven weeks, so I just need something stronger.
Congratulations on the wedding. I definitely want to get you sorted before then. Can I ask a few questions about the headaches first, and then we’ll agree what will actually help?
model.why: Acknowledges the deadline and sets the agenda

model.text: Sure.
The zigzags — do they build up gradually, and do they go away completely before the headache?
They spread over a few minutes, then fade after about twenty. Then the headache — one side, throbbing, I feel sick and can’t stand light.
Have you ever had weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or zigzags that didn’t go away? And have any of these headaches come on suddenly, like a thunderclap?
model.why: Screens for atypical aura and secondary causes

model.text: No, nothing like that. Always the same pattern.
Is this like the migraines you had as a teenager?
No, those were just headaches. No lights. This is new.
And you’re on the combined pill, Rigevidon. What was it started for?
model.why: Links the headache to the contraception

model.text: Heavy, painful periods mainly. It’s been great for that. And obviously for not getting pregnant.
One more question I ask everyone, no judgement at all — do you smoke at the moment?
(Pause.) I’d stopped, but with the wedding stress… about five a day. I haven’t told anyone.
Thank you for being honest. What do you think is causing the headaches?
Stress, I suppose. The visual stuff is just part of it. It’s nothing to do with the pill, is it?
Let me come to that. What’s the thing you’d most hate to happen before the wedding?
model.why: Explores the concern behind the request

model.text: Honestly? Getting pregnant before we’re ready. Or my old periods coming back on the honeymoon. That would be a nightmare.

That really helps. The zigzag lines are called an aura, so these are migraines with aura. They aren’t dangerous in themselves, and we can treat them. But the aura changes one important thing: with the combined pill, the oestrogen in it raises the risk of stroke. So we don’t use that pill for anyone who has aura.
So I have to stop it? Seven weeks before my wedding?
Yes, I’d advise stopping it today. But I promise you won’t be left unprotected or back to your old periods. We swap to a method without oestrogen. There are several, and some also help heavy periods.
model.why: Pairs the bad news with reassurance about her real concern

model.text: Options: a progestogen-only pill you could start straight away. An implant in the arm. Or the hormonal coil, which is the best treatment for heavy periods and is also excellent contraception. The coil and the implant can cause irregular bleeding in the first few months, which matters with the wedding so close. What feels right?
model.why: Safe alternatives, the original indication, and honest timing

model.text: I like the idea of the coil for the periods. But not spotting on my honeymoon.

That’s sensible. One plan is to start the progestogen-only pill today, use condoms until it’s working, and fit the coil after the honeymoon if you still want it. If periods are heavy meanwhile, tranexamic acid or mefenamic acid on the heavy days can help. Would that work?
model.why: Shared decision built around her priorities

model.text: Yes. That actually sounds fine.

For the migraines: a triptan tablet when the headache starts, with ibuprofen or paracetamol, and an anti-sickness tablet if you need it. A headache diary will show whether they’re frequent enough to need a preventer. And I’d really like to help you stop smoking — it adds to the stroke risk too. Would you try the stop-smoking service?
model.why: Acute migraine treatment, diary and smoking support

model.text: I’ll try. My fiancé wants me to stop anyway.

Great. Stop Rigevidon today. Start the new pill and use condoms until I confirm it’s working. If you ever get sudden weakness, face drooping, slurred speech, an aura that doesn’t go away, or a sudden severe headache, that’s 999.
model.why: Specific stroke safety-net and bridging advice

model.text: Okay. That’s a lot, but it makes sense.

I’ll book you with the nurse this week to go through the new pill, and a review before the wedding to see how the headaches are. Just so I know I’ve explained it well — what will you tell your fiancé tonight?
That the zigzag headaches mean I can’t have the combined pill because of stroke risk, I’m switching to a mini-pill, condoms for now, maybe a coil later, and I’m stopping smoking.

social.t: Seven weeks away. Every part of the plan should protect it: no unplanned pregnancy, no return of heavy periods, and awareness of early spotting with some methods.
Wedding stress has triggered a smoking relapse and may be triggering migraines. Both are worth addressing kindly.

legal.t: Group 1 drivers do not usually need to tell the DVLA about migraine; advise her not to drive during an aura or attack.

professional.t: Continuing a UKMEC 4 method after aura has been reported is unsafe prescribing. Document the aura, the advice to stop, the alternative started and the bridging advice (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Offer all suitable non-oestrogen methods with honest information on bleeding patterns, and let her choose timing around the wedding.

community.t: Local stop-smoking service; The Migraine Trust for information; sexual health clinics can fit implants and coils.

redFlags: Aura with weakness, speech disturbance or lasting more than 60 minutes
New aura while on combined hormonal contraception
psychosocial: Wedding in seven weeks and fear of unplanned pregnancy
Reliance on the pill for heavy, painful periods
Smoking relapse under stress, not disclosed
ice: Idea: stress headaches; the visual symptoms are part of it and unrelated to the pill
Concern: pregnancy or heavy periods ruining the wedding and honeymoon

playbook.diagnosis: New migraine with typical visual aura in a 31-year-old on a combined oral contraceptive, who smokes: UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception. Stop the combined pill.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The zigzag lines are an aura, so these are migraines with aura. On their own they’re treatable. But with the oestrogen in your pill they raise the risk of stroke, so we swap to a pill without oestrogen.”

management.reflectIce: “Your biggest worry is the wedding. This plan keeps you protected and your periods under control, without the stroke risk.”
management.psychosocial: Time changes around the wedding; offer stop-smoking support without judgement; involve her fiancé if she wishes.
sharedPlan: Stop Rigevidon today (UKMEC 4); progestogen-only pill now with condoms until effective; LNG-IUS or implant later if she chooses
Heavy periods: LNG-IUS first choice (NICE NG88) or tranexamic and mefenamic acid meanwhile
Migraine: triptan with NSAID or paracetamol, antiemetic if needed (NICE CG150); diary; avoid topiramate (MHRA June 2024)
safetyNet: Sudden weakness, facial droop, speech problems, prolonged aura or thunderclap headache: 999
Nurse contraception review this week; GP review before the wedding

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed on the pill, not the painkiller. The candidate who hears “zigzag lines, then the headache” and thinks of her contraception passes the Tasks domain; the one who also protects her wedding passes the rest.

items.fail: Prescribing a triptan and leaving her on Rigevidon.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception.
items.fix: Ask about contraception in every woman with new aura, and stop the combined pill today.

items.fail: Stopping the pill with “use condoms for now” and nothing else.
items.why: Leaves her exposed to pregnancy and heavy periods seven weeks before her wedding.
items.fix: Start a progestogen-only pill today, bridge with condoms, and plan the heavy periods.

items.why: MHRA (June 2024): contraindicated in women of childbearing potential without a Pregnancy Prevention Programme; it also reduces hormonal contraceptive effect.
items.fix: Use a diary first; if prevention is needed, discuss the other CG150 options.

items.fail: Delivering “stroke risk” bluntly and moving on.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” She hears only that her wedding plans are ruined.
items.fix: Pair it with her concern: “You won’t be unprotected or back to your old periods.”

items.fail: Never asking about smoking, or asking with judgement.
items.why: She hides it, and it is an extra stroke risk.
items.fix: “No judgement — do you smoke at the moment?” Then offer support.

items.fail: Jargon: “UKMEC 4, switch to a POP or LNG-IUS.”
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “A pill without oestrogen”, “the hormonal coil”, “a small rod in the arm”.

timeMap.d: She describes the aura in her opening line. Hear it; don’t jump to painkillers.
Typical, reversible visual aura then migraine. Any motor, speech or persistent symptoms? Thunderclap? New compared with her teens. The pill, why she takes it, and smoking.
She thinks it’s stress. Her real fear: pregnancy or heavy periods ruining the wedding.
Migraine with aura plus oestrogen equals stroke risk: stop today. Progestogen-only pill now, condoms, coil later. Period plan. Triptan plus NSAID. Stop smoking.
Stroke symptoms 999. Nurse this week, review before the wedding. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a triptan or stronger analgesia and leaves her on the combined pill; or stops the pill with no alternative contraception or period plan; never asks about smoking.
wordPics.pass: Recognises migraine with aura, stops the combined pill, arranges a progestogen-only method with condoms in the meantime, treats the migraine and gives a stroke safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: hears the wedding fear and builds the plan around it; addresses heavy periods (LNG-IUS or tranexamic and mefenamic acid) and warns honestly about early irregular bleeding; finds the smoking without judgement; avoids topiramate; teach-back and review before the wedding.

avoid.dont: “Let’s try a triptan and see how you go.”
avoid.instead: “The zigzags change one important thing, and it’s not the painkiller — it’s your pill.”
avoid.why: Treating the headache and missing UKMEC 4 is the key Tasks fail.

avoid.dont: “You’ll have to stop the pill. Use condoms and we’ll see.”
avoid.instead: “You won’t be left unprotected — we swap to a method without oestrogen, starting today.”
avoid.why: Stopping without a replacement leaves her exposed seven weeks before her wedding.

avoid.dont: “Smoking on the pill is really dangerous, you know.”
avoid.instead: “No judgement — lots of people start again under stress. Can I help you stop?”
avoid.why: A lecture shuts down disclosure; support gets her to the service.

I’ll book you with the nurse this week to go through the new pill, and a review before the wedding to see how the headaches are. Just so I know I’ve explained it well — what will you tell your fiancé tonight?
That the zigzag headaches mean I can’t have the combined pill because of stroke risk, I’m switching to a mini-pill, condoms for now, maybe a coil later, and I’m stopping smoking.

SCA_STEM.name: Robyn Carter
pmh: Migraine without aura in her teens
SCA_STEM.recent: BMI 24. On Rigevidon for 6 years. No previous record of migraine with aura.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: headaches with “zigzag lights”; asking for stronger painkillers.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: UKMEC 2025 (CoSRH) · NICE CG150 (updated June 2025) · NICE NG88 · NICE NG209 · MHRA Drug Safety Update (June 2024)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: New migraine with aura in a woman on the combined pill is an absolute contraindication to oestrogen. Stop the combined pill today, and at the same time give her safe contraception, a plan for her periods and migraine treatment.

points.t: NICE CG150: aura is reversible, usually visual (zigzag lines, flickering, a blind spot), develops over at least 5 minutes and lasts 5 to 60 minutes, then a migraine headache follows. Hers fits exactly. It is new: her teenage migraines had no aura.
UKMEC 2025: migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 (unacceptable health risk) for combined hormonal contraception at any age, because of the increased risk of ischaemic stroke. The combined pill must stop.

Progestogen-only methods (pill, implant, injection) and the LNG-IUS can be used with migraine with aura. A progestogen-only pill can usually be started straight away; use condoms until the new method is effective, timing per CoSRH guidance.

points.h: Remember why she was on the pill
points.t: NICE NG88: the LNG-IUS is the first treatment to consider for heavy menstrual bleeding without identified pathology. Warn that bleeding is often irregular in the first few cycles and that benefits may take up to 6 cycles. If she declines, NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid or tranexamic acid can be used.

NICE CG150: offer an oral triptan with an NSAID or paracetamol, and consider an antiemetic. Take the triptan when the headache starts. Keep a headache diary and warn about medication-overuse headache. For prevention, CG150 lists propranolol, topiramate or amitriptyline.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (June 2024): topiramate is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women of childbearing potential unless a Pregnancy Prevention Programme is in place. It also reduces the effect of hormonal contraception. For a woman about to marry, it is a poor first choice.
Smoking adds to stroke risk. Ask without judgement and offer stop-smoking support (NICE NG209).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe the aura in her own words; acknowledged the wedding without accepting “just stronger painkillers”.
Wedding in seven weeks, stress, relapse into smoking, reliance on the pill for heavy periods.
Picked up “vision goes funny, then the headache”, “seven weeks” and the hesitation about smoking.
Idea (stress headaches, pill irrelevant), concern (pregnancy or heavy periods ruining the wedding), expectation (stronger analgesia).
Blood pressure check at the contraception review; no imaging needed for typical aura; headache diary.
Migraine with aura vs TIA vs secondary headache; checked for atypical, prolonged or motor aura and thunderclap onset.
Screened for persistent or motor aura, speech disturbance and sudden severe headache; identified the oestrogen stroke risk.
Named migraine with aura and UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception in plain words.
Stop the combined pill today; progestogen-only pill now with condoms; LNG-IUS option after the wedding; triptan plus NSAID or paracetamol plus antiemetic.
Heavy periods (tranexamic or mefenamic acid; LNG-IUS per NICE NG88); smoking cessation; topiramate avoided.
Stroke symptoms mean 999; nurse appointment this week; review before the wedding; headache diary; teach-back.

social.t: Seven weeks away. Every part of the plan should protect it: no unplanned pregnancy, no return of heavy periods, and awareness of early spotting with some methods.
Wedding stress has triggered a smoking relapse and may be triggering migraines. Both are worth addressing kindly.

legal.t: Group 1 drivers do not usually need to tell the DVLA about migraine; advise her not to drive during an aura or attack.

professional.t: Continuing a UKMEC 4 method after aura has been reported is unsafe prescribing. Document the aura, the advice to stop, the alternative started and the bridging advice (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Offer all suitable non-oestrogen methods with honest information on bleeding patterns, and let her choose timing around the wedding.

community.t: Local stop-smoking service; The Migraine Trust for information; sexual health clinics can fit implants and coils.

redFlags: Aura with weakness, speech disturbance or lasting more than 60 minutes
New aura while on combined hormonal contraception
psychosocial: Wedding in seven weeks and fear of unplanned pregnancy
Reliance on the pill for heavy, painful periods
Smoking relapse under stress, not disclosed
ice: Idea: stress headaches; the visual symptoms are part of it and unrelated to the pill
Concern: pregnancy or heavy periods ruining the wedding and honeymoon

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: New migraine with typical visual aura in a 31-year-old on a combined oral contraceptive, who smokes: UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception. Stop the combined pill.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The zigzag lines are an aura, so these are migraines with aura. On their own they’re treatable. But with the oestrogen in your pill they raise the risk of stroke, so we swap to a pill without oestrogen.”

management.reflectIce: “Your biggest worry is the wedding. This plan keeps you protected and your periods under control, without the stroke risk.”
management.psychosocial: Time changes around the wedding; offer stop-smoking support without judgement; involve her fiancé if she wishes.
sharedPlan: Stop Rigevidon today (UKMEC 4); progestogen-only pill now with condoms until effective; LNG-IUS or implant later if she chooses
Heavy periods: LNG-IUS first choice (NICE NG88) or tranexamic and mefenamic acid meanwhile
Migraine: triptan with NSAID or paracetamol, antiemetic if needed (NICE CG150); diary; avoid topiramate (MHRA June 2024)
safetyNet: Sudden weakness, facial droop, speech problems, prolonged aura or thunderclap headache: 999
Nurse contraception review this week; GP review before the wedding

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed on the pill, not the painkiller. The candidate who hears “zigzag lines, then the headache” and thinks of her contraception passes the Tasks domain; the one who also protects her wedding passes the rest.

items.fail: Prescribing a triptan and leaving her on Rigevidon.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception.
items.fix: Ask about contraception in every woman with new aura, and stop the combined pill today.

items.fail: Stopping the pill with “use condoms for now” and nothing else.
items.why: Leaves her exposed to pregnancy and heavy periods seven weeks before her wedding.
items.fix: Start a progestogen-only pill today, bridge with condoms, and plan the heavy periods.

items.why: MHRA (June 2024): contraindicated in women of childbearing potential without a Pregnancy Prevention Programme; it also reduces hormonal contraceptive effect.
items.fix: Use a diary first; if prevention is needed, discuss the other CG150 options.

items.fail: Delivering “stroke risk” bluntly and moving on.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” She hears only that her wedding plans are ruined.
items.fix: Pair it with her concern: “You won’t be unprotected or back to your old periods.”

items.fail: Never asking about smoking, or asking with judgement.
items.why: She hides it, and it is an extra stroke risk.
items.fix: “No judgement — do you smoke at the moment?” Then offer support.

items.fail: Jargon: “UKMEC 4, switch to a POP or LNG-IUS.”
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “A pill without oestrogen”, “the hormonal coil”, “a small rod in the arm”.
